packets.bounded_proposition: Near the 1300 CE anchor, the later Ibn Khaldun tradition identifies Sākūra as a mawlā/client of the ruling house, and later Mande traditions preserve servile language around Sekure/Sākūra. Some scholarship has rendered this background as slave or freed slave, but specialist source criticism shows that neither the Arabic status term, the later oral terminology, nor the reconstructed early-Mali kinglist can safely carry an exact slave-status classification without qualification. The packet therefore preserves a possible servile/client origin as an unresolved historical status question, not as a secure 1300 territorial-practice claim.
packets.required_abstention: Do not translate mawlā mechanically as slave, treat later Mande servile terminology as an exact thirteenth-century legal category, infer a Mali-wide slavery institution from one ruler's possible social origin, or back-project better-attested mid-fourteenth-century slavery into 1300.
deeper_reasoning: Gomez reproduces Ibn Khaldun's description of Sākūra as a mawlā/client who usurped kingship; the source-native Arabic category is broader than an automatic slave-status translation.
Conrad explicitly treats Sākūra's mawlā description as a social-status problem and discusses alternatives in which the term could encode vassal/first-comer hierarchy rather than literal enslavement.
Austen and Jansen show that the early-Mali kinglist, although detailed and plausible, requires source criticism because Ibn Khaldun's narrative may partly serve a theoretical/exemplary structure.

Austen and Jansen also preserve later Mande traditions with servile-ruler terminology, but those traditions are geographically limited and were recorded much later; they are not independent contemporaneous proof of Sākūra's legal status.
Much of the modern literature ultimately depends on the same small Arabic/oral evidentiary bases, so citation multiplicity must not be mistaken for independent attestations.

Even a secure formerly enslaved individual at the apex of the polity would establish an individual status history, not by itself the prevalence, structure, legality, or selected-year territorial extent of slavery across Mali.
Later fourteenth-century sources such as Ibn Battuta can establish later Mali slavery contexts but do not fill the temporal interval back to the 1300 anchor.
packets.independence_note: The source list is not four independent attestations. Gomez and Levtzion depend materially on Ibn Khaldun for Sākūra; Austen/Jansen and Conrad add source criticism and later Mande oral traditions. The packet therefore treats source families/dependencies explicitly rather than counting publications.
packets.inference_rule: Release Sākūra's status only as an unresolved possible servile/client-origin question. Do not publish positive selected-year Mali territorial slavery from this packet.
